subject: what households do when the municipality stops collecting rubbish, and how comfortable and struggling households cope differently
citation: Kalina M, Makwetu N, Tilley E (2023). 'The rich will always be able to dispose of their waste': a view from the frontlines of municipal failure in Makhanda, South Africa. Environment, Development and Sustainability. doi:10.1007/s10668-023-03363-1

claims.text: Unreliable collection breeds private coping: when the municipality fails to show up, people store waste in yards and bins or hire private collectors, and any new service is judged by whether it reproduces the divide where the rich can always dispose of their waste.
evaluative_rules: Judge a service by whether it reaches everyone equally, not by whether it works for those who can pay
objections: Will this actually reach me, or only the people who can pay for it?
vocabulary: deal with it as it comes
the rich will always be able to dispose of their waste

readings.text: Someone who has seen collection go from weekly to now and again would judge a new service by whether it restores a predictable weekly rhythm, not by whether it adds extra bins or once-off cleanups.

If you have enough black bins to tide you over for a second, third or fourth week, you would weigh a new service mainly on whether it makes your stored waste someone else's problem sooner rather than later.
Someone who already hires a private collector would be less open to a new municipal service unless it proves it can match the reliability of the truck they pay for themselves.

If you believe the municipality starts with rich areas because they are seen as more consistent rate payers, you would judge any new service by whether it visibly reaches your area at the same time as the suburbs, not by whether it exists on paper.

claims.text: Without safe spaces, containers, or transport, burning feels preferable to dumping but still unsafe and time-consuming, so people fall back on dumping and burning, and any new product is read against a landscape of normalised dumping and filth.
evaluative_rules: Judge a disposal option by whether it is safe and reachable without a car or money, not by whether it is ideal
objections: Do I have a safe place to use this, or will I still end up dumping or burning?

readings.text: Someone who has no safe spaces to burn and no bins to use would weigh any new product against whether it removes the need to find a place for waste at all, since both burning and dumping are already blocked.
If burning feels preferable to dumping but is still time-consuming and unsafe, a new product would be read for whether it makes disposal quicker and safer than walking out alone into the veldt.

Someone who sees filth as normal and says the community no longer sees it would be slower to notice a new product's benefit, because the product would be judged against a landscape where rubbish is already a daily occurrence.

If people already fall back on dumping at collection points or in the veldt when bins are filthy or absent, a new product would be weighed by whether it can work without relying on municipal collection or containers.

claims.text: Workers are not the root cause: unpaid salaries and internal grievances sit behind the failure, so residents blame a corrupt, morally bankrupt administration, expect continued failure, and read any new product as a symptom of that corruption rather than a credible fix.
evaluative_rules: Judge a solution by whether it addresses the corrupt administration, not by whether it blames the workers
objections: Is this a real fix, or just another symptom of the same corrupt administration?

readings.text: If residents blame a corrupt, morally bankrupt administration and expect continued failure, they would approach any new product as a symptom of that corruption rather than a credible fix, and would look for signs that it serves the administration rather than them.

Someone who sees unpaid salaries and internal grievances as the reason workers do not pitch would weigh any new product by asking whether it addresses those internal grievances, and would dismiss it if it only deals with the visible service failure.

Someone who says workers are not fundamentally responsible would be open to a new product only if it clearly separates the workers' role from the administration's failures, and would reject it if it blames workers or ignores the administration.

claims.text: Filth becomes normal: when uncollected waste is scattered by animals and seen as a health risk to children, people stop caring about proper disposal and resign themselves to living in filth, so any new product is read against that baseline of normalised filth.
evaluative_rules: Judge a product by whether it can cut through resignation, not by whether it assumes people still care about proper disposal
objections: Will this matter when filth has already become normal?

readings.text: Someone who says the community no longer sees filth because we are living in filth would weigh any new product against whether it can be used without first having to collect and pick up scattered rubbish.

If you have long been suffering when it comes to rubbish and say community members don't care anymore, you would judge a new product mainly by whether it works even where there are no containers and the municipality does not collect.
Someone who worries that children playing in the street could get into medical waste would be more open to a new product only if it reduces the health risk from filth that has become normal.
If you see rubbish strewn all over because donkeys and cows get to it before the van comes around, you would be sceptical of a new product that assumes waste stays where it is put.

claims.text: Unequal prioritisation is the lens: because the municipality starts with rich areas where ratepayers are seen as more consistent, residents judge service delivery as unequal despite shared problems, and any new product is read through that lens of unequal prioritisation.
evaluative_rules: Judge a service by who gets prioritised first, not by whether problems are shared
objections: Will the rich areas get this first while we are left behind?

readings.text: If someone sees the municipality starting with rich areas because ratepayers there are seen as more consistent, they would weigh a new service by whether it is offered first to those same areas or reaches them at the same time.

Someone who argues that not everybody in the location is on Sbonelelo and that they are also ratepayers would weigh a new service by whether it treats their bought houses as deserving of the same priority as the suburbs.

If someone stresses that problems are all the same and that everyone drives on the same roads with potholes, they would weigh a new service by whether it is designed around shared problems rather than separate areas.

Someone who lacks sufficient or secure space to store waste during collection droughts would weigh a new service by whether it shortens the gap between collections, because otherwise they are left with dumping or burning their household waste.

confidence: ethnographic, single municipality, fieldwork in Makhanda — mechanisms durable, magnitudes unknown
year_note: Interviews June to October 2021, Makhanda (Eastern Cape).
